objective.statement: Tell written pitch from concert pitch and say which way, and by how much, each kind of transposing instrument moves a note.
successCriteria: I know written pitch is what is printed and concert pitch is what sounds.
I know B♭, A and F instruments sound a tone, a minor 3rd and a perfect 5th below the written note.
I do not confuse the instrument's name with the key of the music.

explanation.text: Some instruments sound higher or lower than the notes written for them. The double bass sounds an octave lower than written; the piccolo an octave higher. Others sound at other distances. A clarinet in B♭ or a trumpet in B♭ sounds a tone (a major 2nd) lower than written; a clarinet in A sounds a minor 3rd lower; a horn in F or a cor anglais sounds a perfect 5th lower.
The name tells you the note that sounds when the player reads a written C. A B♭ clarinet that reads a C sounds B♭. An A clarinet that reads C sounds A. A horn in F that reads C sounds F.

Musicians therefore separate WRITTEN pitch (the notes printed in the player's part) from CONCERT pitch (the pitch that really sounds). If a piece in G major is played by a piano and a B♭ clarinet, the piano part is written in G, but the clarinet part is written a tone higher, in A major, so that it sounds in G.

Always say which way you are going. From concert pitch to written pitch for these instruments you go UP (by a tone, a minor 3rd or a perfect 5th). From written pitch to concert pitch you go DOWN by the same interval. The name of the instrument (B♭, A or F) is not the key of the music: transpose the key of the music by the interval.
Concert → written: up. Written → concert: down. B♭: a tone. A: a minor 3rd. F: a perfect 5th.

music.textAlternative: A four-note phrase in G major at concert pitch.

steps: This phrase is at concert pitch, in G major.
A clarinet in B♭ needs it written a tone higher.
G major up a tone is A major.
demonstration.textAlternative: A phrase in G major; the written clarinet part is in A major.

guided.prompt: An instrument “in B♭” sounds how far BELOW the note that is written for it?

A.reason: That is the distance for an instrument in A, not for one in B♭.

F.reason: That is the distance for an instrument in F, not for one in B♭.

C.reason: That is the distance for an instrument in C an octave lower, not for one in B♭.

hints: B♭ sounds a tone lower than written, A a minor 3rd, F a perfect 5th.
B♭ instruments sound a tone lower than written, A instruments a minor 3rd lower, F instruments a perfect 5th lower.

feedback.correct: Yes: the interval belongs to the instrument.

mistakes.wrong-octave: Check the octave: the new version should be exactly one octave higher or lower — not the same pitch, and not two octaves away.
mistakes.wrong-clef: Look at which clef the question asks for — alto and tenor clefs are easy to mix up.
mistakes.wrong-interval: B♭ is a tone, A a minor 3rd and F a perfect 5th.
mistakes.wrong-direction: Written pitch is higher than concert pitch for these instruments.
mistakes.key-signature-missing: A transposed part needs the key signature of its new key.
mistakes.accidental-not-adjusted: Accidentals change too. Work out what each altered note is in the original key, then find the same degree in the new key.
mistakes.enharmonic-respelling: Move every letter by the same number of steps.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Transpose the key first, then each note, then check accidentals.
